summary: Radar for 2026-10-16. Every candidate is a GLP-1 topic. 1) Best new opportunity: a peer-reviewed JAMA Network Open study (Oct 15, Penn team) used AI to analyse Reddit posts from about 40,000 users. People who said they were taking unapproved "retatrutide" most often reported more appetite, poor sleep and a fast heart rate, not the stomach side effects seen in the trials. The researchers say they can't confirm what those people actually took. This fits our best-performing lane (gray-market warnings: bootleg Reta got 128 views) and gives it an evergreen science angle. Medscape and Medical Xpress covered it within 24 h, and there are few creator videos so far. 2) Tirzepatide muscle remains our strongest evergreen series; next up is strength training. 3) Named next-gen decoder: Foundayo (orforglipron) vs oral semaglutide in ACHIEVE-3 (Lancet), back in the news Oct 14. 4) Fresh hooks for named drugs, all observational: semaglutide and fewer asthma/COPD flare-ups (ERS data, new press Oct 15); a SELECT analysis finding semaglutide's heart benefit isn't fully explained by weight lost (adults with heart disease and overweight/obesity); a calm tirzepatide eye-health explainer (lower diabetic retinopathy risk vs lifestyle alone, observational, plus the absolute ION risk from Annals: about 3–4 extra cases per 10,000 over 18 months); the "why some people lose 20% and others barely lose any" responder question. 5) Seasonal: US open enrollment and Jan 1 coverage changes (BCBS Michigan dropping obesity coverage; Walmart's $0 GLP-1s for 2027 apply only to employees with type 2 diabetes). Use a "questions for your prescriber and plan" angle and never point to cheaper sources. Rejected: the CNN story on prescribing to people with anorexia (risk of encouraging eating disorders), the low-dose tirzepatide strategy paper (dosing), and compounded price or online-program roundups. Facts checked: the MHRA £2M seizure headline is GOV.UK, Oct 15. A separate Northampton raid in Oct 2025 was valued at £250k+, so don't mix the two up. Walmart's benefit is limited to type 2 diabetes. ACHIEVE-3 compared diabetes doses of oral semaglutide (7/14 mg), not the Wegovy pill.

candidates.topic: What Reddit users on unapproved 'retatrutide' reported: JAMA Netw Open study (Oct 15, 2026) found increased appetite, insomnia and fast heart rate topped the list, unlike the GI-dominated trial results
candidates.angle: Calm 'what's confirmed vs not' decoder: researchers analysed ~40,000 Reddit users with AI. The top reports (more appetite, poor sleep, fast heart rate) don't match Lilly's trials, and the authors say 'we can't verify exactly what they're taking.' Evergreen payoff: why a 'research peptide' isn't the trial drug. Retatrutide is investigational, not approved anywhere as of Oct 2026. Talk to a prescriber about approved options. Never name sellers.
candidates.why_now: Published in a peer-reviewed journal Oct 15 and picked up by Medscape and Medical Xpress within hours. It lands on top of this week's bootleg-Reta death-report coverage (CBS, Oct 13) and Lilly's lawsuits, with Lilly earnings on Oct 29. People search 'retatrutide side effects' constantly, and few creator videos cover the study yet.

evidence.signal: JAMA Netw Open, Oct 15, 2026: ~40,000 Reddit users, 7,823 with classifiable symptoms; appetite increase most common; authors caution products unverified

candidates.topic: Mounjaro (tirzepatide) and your eyes: lower diabetic retinopathy risk vs lifestyle alone (observational), plus what the new Annals study says about rare optic-nerve risk
candidates.angle: Balanced 'does tirzepatide affect my eyes?' Short. Open with the cohort finding: tirzepatide starters with diabetes and overweight/obesity had lower 12-month retinopathy risk than matched lifestyle-only patients (86,923 per group). Then give the calm absolute figure from Annals: about 3–4 extra ischemic optic neuropathy cases per 10,000 over 18 months, adults 18–65 with type 2 diabetes. Action: tell your eye doctor you're on a GLP-1 and report sudden vision changes promptly. Not a scare piece.
candidates.why_now: ScienceDaily (Oct 15) and Fox's 'went blind' story are driving searches. Medical Economics (Oct 15) re-surfaced the tirzepatide eye-protection finding. Our data say scare framing lands low, so the balanced 'what helps' angle with a named drug is the way in.
